passage:
Sunday, late. Spent two hours watching that fitness guy with the eight-pack again. Every reel ends the same way: 'Want this body? Link in bio, special discount on my shred plan.' I kept looking at my own arms and feeling like a flat tyre. I even asked Mum for money for his plan. Then Rafiq said something at cricket that stuck: 'The man earns every time you feel bad about yourself.' Tonight I checked. Every single post sells something: powder, plan, gloves, a 'secret' app. He needs me to feel not enough. So I tried an experiment. Unfollowed him and four others like him. Followed the sports physio our coach recommends, who posts about sleep, warm-ups and injuries and never shows off a stomach. Weird, but I feel calmer already. Still a bit jealous of those arms, honestly. But I'm not paying to feel worse.
- Pranav

qa.q: How does every reel from the fitness influencer end?
qa.a: With an offer: 'Want this body? Link in bio', and a discount on his shred plan.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling while watching those arms in the reels?
qa.a: Pranav felt envious and inadequate, 'like a flat tyre', and still admits to being a bit jealous.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Pranav, and why?
qa.a: Unfollowing accounts that profit from insecurity and following an evidence-based physio, which already left Pranav calmer 🙂

qa.q: How might the influencer see Pranav's feeling of not being enough?
qa.a: As a sales opportunity: every time a viewer feels inadequate, the influencer earns from plans and powders.

grounding: A diary showing a teen envying fitness influencers, checking who profits from that feeling of inadequacy, and choosing evidence-based accounts.

passage: Early March. Hafsa wrote down every bite in a notes app now, adding up numbers in her head through maths class. Between periods she checked her stomach in the washroom mirror, sideways, then again, then again. The next Friday. At her cousin's engagement, Hafsa refused the biryani for an hour, then ate plate after plate so fast she barely tasted it. Afterwards she sat locked in the bathroom, shaking, feeling as if food had taken over her whole brain. Two weeks later. She knocked on the counsellor's door before she could change her mind. 'I think something's wrong with how I eat,' she said. Ms Sharmila listened to all of it, then said, 'Telling me this early took real strength, Hafsa.' With Hafsa's permission, she called Ammi into school that afternoon, and together they booked a doctor's appointment. Walking out, Hafsa felt scared, but lighter.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa check her stomach between periods?
qa.a: In the washroom mirror, sideways, then again and again.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling after the engagement meal?
qa.a: She felt shaken, ashamed and out of control, as if food had taken over her whole brain.

qa.q: Why was going to the counsellor a wise step for Hafsa?
qa.a: The counting and loss of control were warning signs, and speaking early meant an adult and a doctor could help sooner.

qa.q: How does Ms Sharmila see Hafsa's knock on the door?
qa.a: She sees it as strength, not weakness, and acts that day by calling Ammi and helping book a doctor.

grounding: Shows a teen whose food counting and mirror checking spiral, and who speaks to a counsellor early, leading to a doctor's appointment.

passage: Chinmay, you asked why I never let anyone joke about diets at this table. Sit, I'll tell you. When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, I cut photos of thin actresses out of magazines and pasted them inside my cupboard door. I wrote down everything I ate in a little blue diary and checked the long mirror on the landing ten, twenty times a day. At weddings I would eat nothing, then everything, then feel like a stranger was living in my head. One evening my Bua found the diary. I was so ashamed I cried. She didn't scold. She said, 'Usha, this is bigger than you. Let's go to Dr Mehta together.' We went that same week. It took time, and help, but I got better. So remember what your Usha Aaji learned: when food starts to feel like it's running you, tell someone early. Asking is strength.

qa.q: What did Usha paste inside the cupboard door?
qa.a: Photos of thin actresses cut out of magazines.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Bua found the diary?
qa.a: Usha felt so ashamed that tears came, after a long time of feeling out of control around food.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Usha's story?
qa.a: Bua finding the diary and taking Usha to Dr Mehta that same week, which turned a secret into early help.

qa.q: How did Bua see the blue diary?
qa.a: Bua saw it as a sign of something bigger than Usha could handle alone, needing a doctor rather than a scolding.

grounding: An elder's story of food counting, mirror checking and feeling out of control around food, and getting a doctor's help early.

passage: The clinic waiting room smelled of disinfectant and the TV was stuck on a cooking show. Sachin's mother, Sudha, nudged him when a man walked past with a paunch. 'See, beta, that's where too many samosas lead. You've got a little round yourself since the exams.' Two aunties across the row looked over. Sachin's face burned. He wanted to say nothing, like always. Instead he leaned closer. 'Ma, I know you mean it for my health. But when you say it in front of people, it really stings. I end up hating how I look.' Sudha blinked. 'I didn't think it hurt you like that.' She was quiet for a while. 'Then tell me how to say it.' 'Say let's do something together. Like evening walks, instead of comments.' She squeezed his arm. 'Walks after dinner, then. Both of us. My knees need it too.'

qa.q: What was on the TV in the clinic waiting room?
qa.a: It was stuck on a cooking show.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when his mother commented in front of people?
qa.a: His face burned with embarrassment and the remark stung, leaving him hating how he looked.

qa.q: What went right in how Sachin responded?
qa.a: He named the hurt calmly, said he knew she meant well, and suggested a shared habit like evening walks instead of comments.

qa.q: How does Sudha see her comment at first, and after Sachin speaks?
qa.a: At first she thinks it's harmless health advice; after hearing him, she sees it hurt and asks how to say it better.

grounding: Shows a teen stung by his mother's well-meant weight comment, telling her how it feels and agreeing on walks together.

passage:
Dear Appa,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it out loud, I start crying and you think I'm being dramatic.
Every time I come back from basketball, you say, 'Again in the sun? You're getting so dark, kanna. Look at Keerthana, how fair she stayed.' I know you say it because you love me and worry about how people will see me. But it stings every single time. Last week I skipped practice just so you wouldn't say it.
Could you say 'Did you win?' instead? Or 'Drink water, you look tired'? Those I'd love to hear.
And if you're worried about my health, let's do something together. Come and watch a match, or we could start cycling on Sunday mornings like we used to.
I love basketball, Appa. I don't want to give it up for a colour.
Love,
your daughter, Yamini

qa.q: What does Appa usually say when Yamini comes back from basketball?
qa.a: He says, 'Again in the sun? You're getting so dark, kanna,' and compares her to Keerthana.

qa.q: Why did Yamini skip practice last week?
qa.a: She felt so stung and ashamed by the comments on her skin that she avoided practice to escape them.

qa.q: What kinder words does Yamini ask for, and why might they work?
qa.a: 'Did you win?' or 'Drink water', which show care for her and her health without judging her colour 🙂

qa.q: How might Appa see his own comments?
qa.a: He likely sees them as loving protection from what others might say, not realising how much they hurt her.

grounding: A letter from a teen to her father, telling him how his well-meant comments on her complexion sting and asking for kinder words and shared habits.

passage:
'I can't wear this lehenga on stage. My arms look huge,' Vandana said, tugging at the sleeves in the changing room.
'You look fine, Vandu. Honestly.'
'You're just saying that.'
Sarita sat down on the bench. 'Okay, can I tell you something? I hate my teeth. I've practised smiling with my mouth closed for two years.'
Vandana stared. 'Your teeth? But you smile all the time.'
'Closed-mouth, though. Did you ever notice?'
'...No. Never.'
'Exactly. Nobody's staring at the thing we're staring at.'
Vandana laughed, a little shakily. 'So we're both walking around hiding something.'
'Yeah. But that's not why I like dancing with you. You never miss a beat, and you always count me in when I freeze.'
Vandana let go of the sleeves. 'And you're the one who makes me laugh backstage. Teeth or no teeth.'
From the door, the dance teacher called, 'Sarita, Vandana, girls of group three, you're on!'

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after Sarita talked about her teeth?

passage: Last winter, the week before the class photo, I stopped going to the canteen. My acne had flared across my chin, and when my brother Arnab joked that I looked like a pepperoni pizza, I believed every word. My friend Moumita found me eating lunch alone behind the library. 'Seema, your skin looks fine to me,' she said. I rolled my eyes. Then she did something I didn't expect. She pushed up her sleeve and showed me the stretch marks on her arm. 'I wore full sleeves all summer because of these. I still do sometimes.' I remember the relief, like someone had opened a window. We sat there listing the things we hide, laughing a bit. She never once said I was pretty. She said she missed my stupid jokes in the canteen. The next day I went back, chin and all.

qa.q: Where did Moumita find Seema eating lunch?
qa.a: Alone behind the library.

qa.q: What did Seema feel when Moumita showed the stretch marks?
qa.a: Seema felt a wave of relief and less alone, 'like someone had opened a window'.

qa.q: Why did Moumita's support help more than just saying 'you look fine'?
qa.a: She shared her own insecurity honestly and valued Seema's jokes and company, not appearance.

qa.q: How does Moumita see her own full sleeves?
qa.a: She sees them as her way of hiding stretch marks, a worry she still carries sometimes.

grounding: A first-person memory of feeling less alone when a friend shared her own insecurity and valued the narrator's company over looks.

'Go without me,' Hemant called through the bathroom door. 'My face is all puffy and this shirt looks terrible.'
'It's the final. We need our goalkeeper,' Asif said.
'I look like a balloon today.'

'What?'
'I'd tell you it's one bad day. That your face doesn't catch the ball. That you're allowed to feel a bit rubbish and still show up.'

Hemant breathed out slowly. 'I don't have to like how I look today. It can just be okay.'
He opened the door, gloves already in his hand.
'Ready?'

passage: The morning of Kalyani's birthday picnic last month, I nearly didn't go. I'd tried on four outfits and hated all of them; my stomach felt huge, my hair wouldn't sit, and I'd already typed 'sorry, fever' to cancel. Then I thought about what I'd say if Kalyani sent me that message about herself. I'd never tell her she looked awful. I'd say, 'Wear the comfy one and come, we just want you there.' So I said it to myself, out loud, feeling a bit silly in front of the mirror. I didn't suddenly love my stomach. I didn't need to. I just decided it was a normal body having a meh day. I deleted the message, put on the old green kurta and caught the bus. We played frisbee till sunset, and I barely thought about my stomach again. I'm Vinita, and I'm learning okay is enough.

qa.q: What message had Vinita typed to cancel the picnic?
qa.a: 'sorry, fever'.

qa.q: How was Vinita feeling while trying on outfits that morning?
qa.a: Vinita felt low and self-critical, hating every outfit and ready to fake a fever to avoid going.

qa.q: What did Vinita try that turned the morning around?
qa.a: Saying out loud the kind words that would be offered to Kalyani, then settling for 'normal body, meh day' and going.

qa.q: What would Kalyani have missed if Vinita had sent that message?
qa.a: She would have missed a friend at her birthday picnic, when all she wanted was Vinita there, not a perfect outfit.

grounding: A first-person account of a bad body day where the narrator speaks to themself like a friend, settles for neutral and goes ahead with plans.

passage: Class teacher's notes, Aparna Menon, 9C, Friday. Madhav has been sitting out of football for two weeks. Today I found out why. While the boys lined up for the team photo, he hung back, and I overheard him ask Joel whether he'd 'ever get a real voice'. Most of the class have shot up this year; Madhav is still one of the smallest, and his voice hasn't dropped. Later, in the empty classroom, I asked how he was. Eyes on his shoes, he said he felt like a little kid next to everyone. I told him bodies grow on their own timetables, some early, some late, and none of it is a race. I also mentioned I'd been the last in my class to grow, which made him smile. I've asked the PE teacher to put him back in goal on Monday and given him a puberty booklet from the school nurse.

qa.q: What did Madhav ask Joel before the team photo?
qa.a: He asked whether he'd ever get a real voice.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling next to his classmates?
qa.a: He felt small and embarrassed, like a little kid next to everyone who had shot up.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Madhav?
qa.a: By explaining bodies grow on their own timetables, sharing a personal memory, and getting him back in goal with a booklet from the nurse.

qa.q: What would change if Madhav had grown early instead?
qa.a: He might feel just as awkward for standing out in a different way, which shows no timetable is the 'right' one.

grounding: A teacher's note on a teen comparing his later puberty with classmates and being reassured that bodies develop at different speeds.

passage:
Thursday. Dear diary, swimming class was awful again. I'm the only one in our group whose body has properly changed already, and I spent the whole hour with a towel wrapped round me. Sunaina is still tiny, and she kept saying she wished she looked like me, which is funny because I wish I looked like her. At home I stood in front of the mirror comparing myself to the girls in our group, one by one. Then Mummy knocked. I told her, and she laughed gently, not at me. 'Beti, at your age I was the last one. Your Masi was the first. We both hated it.' She said bodies don't read the same calendar and nobody wins a prize for being early or late. I felt a bit better. Tomorrow I'm leaving the towel on the bench, at least for the first lap.
- Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila keep wrapped around her during swimming class?
qa.a: A towel, for the whole hour.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel so uncomfortable at the pool?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and alone, being the only one in her group whose body had already changed.

qa.q: What small step could help Sharmila feel easier at the pool?
qa.a: Leaving the towel on the bench for the first lap, a patient start rather than forcing herself to feel fine at once 🙂

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to see Sharmila's body?
qa.a: Sunaina wishes she looked like Sharmila, showing the two are comparing in opposite directions.

grounding: A diary showing a teen comparing her early puberty with others and learning from her mother that bodies develop at different speeds.

passage: In the first week of the college bus from Wadgaon to the taluka town, Madhuri stopped speaking her village Marathi. The town girls laughed at words like 'lai bhari', so she copied their neat, careful sentences and kept her bajra bhakri wrapped in her bag until she got home, hungry. By the third week her jaw ached from smiling at jokes she didn't find funny. One afternoon Avni from the back seat pulled out her own tiffin. 'My Aaji's thecha. Too spicy for these town people,' she grinned, in full village Marathi. Madhuri laughed before she could stop herself. 'Lai bhari,' she said, and unwrapped her bhakri. They shared it all the way home. Madhuri still used some town words in class; they were useful there. But on the bus she talked like herself, and the girls who smirked mattered a little less every day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri keep wrapped in her bag?
qa.a: Her bajra bhakri, until she got home, hungry.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as her jaw ached from smiling?
qa.a: She felt tired and hollow, pretending to enjoy jokes just to belong.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Madhuri, and why?
qa.a: Keeping some town words for class but talking like herself on the bus, so she fits in lightly without hiding who she is.

grounding: Shows a teen who hides her dialect and food to fit in, then adapts lightly while keeping her core with a friend who accepts it.

passage: The counsellor's room at St Joseph's had a dripping air conditioner and a jar of mints nobody ate. Saurabh sat turning a mint over in his fingers for five minutes before he spoke. 'I don't know what's wrong with me. My friend Tejas... when he talks to a girl, I feel weird. Jealous. Not a friend kind of jealous. And then I'm scared I'm... I don't even know the word.' The counsellor, Mrs Pillai, didn't flinch. 'Nothing's wrong with you, Saurabh. Lots of people your age feel unsure about who they're drawn to. You don't have to pick a label today, or this year.' He let out a breath he hadn't known he was holding. She wrote down a helpline run by trained counsellors and the name of a book in the school library, instead of the random videos he'd been watching at night. 'You can come back any Thursday,' she said. Saurabh pocketed the mint.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai write down for Saurabh?
qa.a: A helpline run by trained counsellors and the name of a book in the school library.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he turned the mint over?
qa.a: He felt scared and confused about his feelings for Tejas, unsure there was even a word for them.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai's response get right?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said nothing was wrong with him, removed pressure to label, and pointed him to reliable information and a safe place to return.

qa.q: What would change if Saurabh had only kept watching random videos at night?
qa.a: He might take in confusing or frightening messages alone, instead of calm facts from a safe adult.

grounding: Shows a teen confused and afraid about attraction who finds a safe counsellor, is told no label is needed yet, and gets reliable information.

passage:

You said at Eid I could write to you about anything, so here goes. I'm confused about myself and it's scaring me. Everyone in my class talks about which boy they like, and I just nod along. passage:

'I promise. What happened?'
'Nothing happened. It's... I think I like girls. Not boys. I've known for a while.'
Trisha felt her own heartbeat. She put her chai down. 'Okay. Thank you for telling me.'
'That's it? You're not freaking out?'
'I'm a bit surprised. But you're still Chandu. Same person who stole my pen in Class 6.'
Chandrika laughed, then her eyes filled. 'Nobody else knows. Not even my sister.'
'Then nobody hears it from me. Not the group, not anyone. It's yours to tell, when you want.'
'Even Rhea? You tell Rhea everything.'
'Not this. This isn't mine.'
Chandrika leaned her head on Trisha's shoulder. 'I was so scared you'd look at me differently.'
'I'm looking at you exactly the same. Maybe a bit prouder.'

passage: I'm Noor, and last spring my friend Leela told me something on the walk home from tuition that I still think about. We'd stopped under the gulmohar near the petrol pump, and Leela said, very fast, 'I don't really feel like a girl or a boy. I've been reading about it for a year. With you, can I just be Leela, and can you say "they"?' I didn't have a clever answer. I said, 'Okay. Thank you for trusting me,' and then, 'Will you tell me when I get it wrong?' Leela nodded, shoulders dropping like a heavy bag had been set down. The hardest part came later, when our group chat asked what we'd talked about for so long. I said it was private and changed the subject. It wasn't my story to tell. Looking back, I think the most useful thing I did was simply not look away.

qa.q: Where did Leela share this with Noor?
qa.a: Under the gulmohar near the petrol pump, on the walk home from tuition.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling in that moment under the gulmohar?
qa.a: Noor felt caught off guard, without a clever answer, but caring and honoured to be trusted.

qa.q: How did Noor handle the group chat's question, and why was it right?
qa.a: Noor said it was private and changed the subject, because Leela's story was not Noor's to share.

qa.q: How did Leela experience Noor's response?
qa.a: Leela felt relieved and accepted, shoulders dropping like a heavy bag had been set down.

grounding: A first-person memory of a friend sharing a private truth about gender, and the narrator listening, keeping the confidence and being a safe person.

qa.a: She may be shocked and frightened by news she didn't expect; her reaction reflects her own fears, not Madhav's worth.

grounding: Shows a teen heartbroken by his family's harsh reaction to who he is, reaching a counsellor and helpline and being reminded it is not his worth.

passage: When Deepika came home from the kasba with her long braid cut short, Dadi screamed as if someone had died. 'What will the whole village say? A girl who looks like a boy!' Papa said nothing at first. Then he told her she had shamed the family and wasn't to go to kabaddi practice again. Deepika sat by the cattle shed till dark, her chest aching, running her fingers through her short hair. Every name Dadi had called her rang in her head. In the morning at school she went to Parveen ma'am, who coached the girls' kabaddi team. Parveen ma'am listened to all of it, then said, 'You are not a shame, Deepika. Your hair and your game are yours.' She checked Deepika felt safe at home, gave her the number of a helpline for girls, and that evening came to the house with the headmistress to talk calmly with Papa.

qa.q: What did Papa forbid Deepika from doing?
qa.a: Going to kabaddi practice again.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling by the cattle shed?
qa.a: She felt heartbroken and ashamed, her chest aching as Dadi's words rang in her head.

qa.q: Which choice helped Deepika most, and why?
qa.a: Going to Parveen ma'am, a safe adult who reminded her of her worth, checked her safety and spoke to the family.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Deepika's short hair?
qa.a: Dadi sees it as a threat to the family's name in the village, fearing what others will say more than seeing Deepika.

grounding: Shows a teen heartbroken by her family's harsh reaction to how she presents herself, finding a safe teacher and helpline and learning it is not her worth.
